question: What is a binary tree and what are its traversal methods?
title: Binary Tree Traversals Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: A **binary tree** is a tree where each node has at most two children. The three DFS traversals: **Inorder** (left-root-right), **Preorder** (root-left-right), **Postorder** (left-right-root). Inorder of a BST gives sorted order — a critical property.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the traversal orders and their use cases, especially inorder=sorted for BST
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the traversal orders or not knowing that inorder of a BST is sorted
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name a practical use for each traversal: inorder=sorted output, preorder=copy/serialize, postorder=delete/calculate subtree size

sections.title: Three DFS Traversals
sections.content: **Inorder (L-Root-R)**: visits left subtree, then root, then right subtree. For a BST, this gives elements in **sorted ascending order**. **Preorder (Root-L-R)**: visits root first — useful for copying or serializing a tree. **Postorder (L-R-Root)**: visits root last — useful when you need children processed before parent (e.g., deleting a tree, calculating subtree sizes). **BFS (Level-order)**: uses a queue, visits nodes level by level.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Inorder: left → root → right (BST → sorted output)
- Preorder: root → left → right (tree copy, serialization)
- Postorder: left → right → root (tree deletion, subtree calculations)
- BFS/Level-order: uses Queue, visits level by level
- All DFS traversals: O(n) time, O(h) space where h = tree height
- Balanced tree height: O(log n); worst case skewed: O(n)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A binary tree has at most two children per node. The three depth-first traversals are: inorder which visits left subtree, then root, then right — for a BST this gives sorted output; preorder which visits root first, then left and right — useful for serialization; and postorder which visits children before the root — useful for deleting or computing subtree values. There's also breadth-first or level-order traversal which uses a queue. The most important property to remember is that inorder traversal of a BST produces a sorted sequence.

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app solving common interview DSA problems
sections.hook: Binary tree traversals show up in nearly every interview — and confusing the three orders is one of the most common mistakes freshers make.

beats.text: A binary tree is just a tree where each node has at most two children — a left child and a right child. The structure itself has no ordering rule; that comes from BSTs.

beats.intro: There are three depth-first traversals, each with a different visit order:
items: Inorder — left, root, right. For a BST this produces sorted ascending output, which is its most useful property.
Preorder — root, left, right. You visit the root first, making it great for copying or serializing a tree.
Postorder — left, right, root. Children are processed before the parent, so it's used for deleting a tree or computing subtree sizes.

beats.text: There's also level-order, which is BFS. It uses a queue and visits nodes level by level instead of going deep first. All DFS traversals run in O(n) time and use O(h) space for the call stack, where h is the tree height.

candidates miss: the practical use case for each traversal. Interviewers love asking 'why preorder and not inorder?' Knowing that preorder captures the root before children — exactly what you need for serialization — sets your answer apart.

sections.cap: Remember the mnemonic: In-Pre-Post tells you where the root fits — In the middle, Pre before, Post after children.

question: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST) and what are its properties?
title: Binary Search Tree BST Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: A **BST** is a binary tree where for every node: all values in the **left subtree are smaller** and all values in the **right subtree are larger**. This property enables O(log n) search, insert, and delete on a balanced BST.

interviewer_intent.testing: BST definition, search algorithm, and awareness of balance requirement for O(log n)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not mentioning that an unbalanced BST degrades to O(n) — a sorted insertion creates a linked list
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention TreeMap in Java which is a Red-Black Tree (self-balancing BST) guaranteeing O(log n)

sections.title: BST Property and Search
sections.content: **BST invariant**: for any node N, every node in N's left subtree has value < N.value, and every node in N's right subtree has value > N.value. To search: start at root, if target < current go left, if target > current go right, if equal — found. On a **balanced** BST this eliminates half the tree per step → O(log n). On an unbalanced BST (e.g., inserting 1,2,3,4,5 in sorted order), it degrades to a linked list → O(n).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- BST property: left < root < right (for every node)
- Inorder traversal of BST = sorted sequence
- Balanced BST: search/insert/delete = O(log n)
- Unbalanced (skewed) BST: degrades to O(n)
- Java's TreeMap and TreeSet use Red-Black Tree (self-balancing BST)
- Red-Black Tree guarantees O(log n) worst case
- BST search is essentially binary search on a tree

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A BST is a binary tree with the invariant that all values in the left subtree are less than the root, and all values in the right subtree are greater. This lets you search by halving the remaining space at each node — similar to binary search — giving O(log n) for a balanced tree. The critical caveat is balance: if you insert sorted data into a BST without balancing, it becomes a linked list with O(n) operations. Java's TreeMap and TreeSet avoid this by using a Red-Black Tree, which is a self-balancing BST that guarantees O(log n) in the worst case.

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app solving common interview DSA problems
sections.hook: A BST sounds simple, but one detail about balance trips up most freshers — and interviewers know exactly where to push.

beats.text: A BST is a binary tree with one core rule: for every node, every value in the left subtree is smaller and every value in the right subtree is larger. That invariant holds for every node in the tree, not just the root.

That rule makes searching fast. You start at the root, and at each step you go left if the target is smaller or right if it's larger. You're eliminating half the remaining nodes at each step — exactly like binary search — giving O(log n) time.

sharp edge: balance is required for O(log n). If you insert numbers in sorted order — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — every new node goes to the right, and you end up with a linked list. Search becomes O(n). This is the most common missed point.
Java's TreeMap and TreeSet handle this for you. They use a Red-Black Tree, which is a self-balancing BST that guarantees O(log n) in the worst case regardless of insertion order.

sections.cap: The formula is: BST property plus balance equals O(log n). Without balance, a BST is just a slow linked list.

question: How do you find the height of a binary tree recursively?
title: Height of Binary Tree Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Height = 1 + max(height of left subtree, height of right subtree).** Base case: null node returns -1 (or 0 depending on convention). This recursive solution is O(n) time because it visits every node once.

interviewer_intent.testing: Recursive thinking on trees — the classic 'trust the recursion' pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting confused by the base case (null node height convention: -1 vs 0) or forgetting to add 1 for the current node
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the recursion intuitively: 'I trust that the recursive call gives me the correct height of each subtree, so I just pick the max and add 1'

sections.title: Recursive Height Calculation
sections.content: The height of a tree is the **longest path from root to a leaf**. Recursively: `height(node) = 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))`. **Base case**: `if (node == null) return -1` (using -1 so a single leaf node has height 0) or `return 0` (so leaf has height 1) — clarify with interviewer which convention they prefer. Either is acceptable as long as you're consistent.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Formula: height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right))
- Base case: null node returns -1 (leaf = height 0) or 0 (leaf = height 1)
- Time: O(n) — visits every node exactly once
- Space: O(h) — recursion stack depth equals tree height
- Diameter of tree uses similar recursive pattern
- This is a postorder traversal — children computed before root

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Finding height is a classic recursion problem on trees. The insight is: the height of any node is 1 plus the maximum height of its two subtrees. The base case is when the node is null — I return -1 by convention so that a single leaf node correctly returns height 0. Then I recursively get the height of the left and right subtrees, take the max, and add 1. This visits every node exactly once so it's O(n) time and O(h) space for the recursion stack where h is the height. I'd always state the base case clearly before writing the recursive case.

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app solving common interview DSA problems
sections.hook: Tree height is the gateway recursion question — nail the base case and the rest writes itself.

beats.text: Height is the length of the longest path from the root down to a leaf. The recursive formula is elegant: the height of any node equals 1 plus the maximum height of its left and right subtrees.

The trick is trusting the recursion. You don't need to think about the whole tree. Just say: assume my recursive calls return the correct height for each subtree, pick the larger one, and add 1 for the current node.

candidates miss: the base case convention. If you return -1 for a null node, a single leaf node correctly gets height 0 — which is the more common convention. If you return 0 for null, a leaf gets height 1. Either works, but you must state which one you're using and stay consistent.

Complexity is O(n) time because you visit every node exactly once, and O(h) space for the recursion stack. Notice this is a postorder traversal — you compute children before you use the results at the parent.

sections.cap: State your base case first, then the recursive formula. That order of explanation is exactly what interviewers want to hear.

question: How does level-order traversal (BFS) work on a binary tree?
title: Level Order Traversal BFS Binary Tree | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Level-order traversal visits nodes level by level using a Queue.** Add root to queue, then repeatedly dequeue a node, process it, and enqueue its children. This is BFS applied to a tree — O(n) time and O(n) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can connect BFS to the queue data structure and apply it to trees
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to do level-order with recursion and DFS instead of recognizing it requires a queue
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how to capture results level by level (queue size trick) to return a list of lists

sections.title: Queue-Based BFS on Trees
sections.content: Add root to queue. While queue is not empty: dequeue a node, process it (add to result), enqueue left child if not null, enqueue right child if not null. **To capture level-by-level results**: at the start of each outer iteration, record `size = queue.size()` — that's how many nodes are on the current level. Process exactly `size` nodes in the inner loop before moving to the next level.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Core structure: Queue + while loop
- Enqueue root, process children, enqueue their children
- Level capture trick: snapshot queue.size() at start of each level
- Time: O(n), Space: O(w) where w = max width (can be O(n) for complete tree)
- BFS finds shortest path — level-order finds depth of a node
- Common variant: return List<List<Integer>> — one inner list per level

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Level-order traversal is BFS applied to a tree and it requires a queue. I add the root to the queue, then loop while the queue is not empty — dequeue a node, add its value to my result, then enqueue its left and right children if they exist. To group results by level, I capture the queue size at the start of each outer iteration — that tells me how many nodes are on the current level — and process exactly that many nodes before incrementing the level. This is O(n) time and O(n) space in the worst case for a full level.

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app solving common interview DSA problems
sections.hook: Level-order traversal is just BFS with a queue — once you see the pattern, it's hard to forget.

beats.text: Level-order traversal visits nodes layer by layer — all nodes at depth 0, then depth 1, then depth 2, and so on. The data structure that makes this work is a queue, because queues process things in the order they arrive.

The algorithm is: add the root to the queue. Then loop while the queue isn't empty — dequeue a node, record its value, enqueue its left child if it exists, enqueue its right child if it exists. That's the entire algorithm.

non-obvious: how to group results by level. Before each iteration, snapshot the current queue size. That number tells you exactly how many nodes are on the current level. Process precisely that many nodes in an inner loop, collect them into a sublist, then move on. This queue-size trick appears in many tree problems.

Complexity is O(n) time and O(w) space where w is the maximum width of the tree. For a complete binary tree, the bottom level can hold roughly n divided by 2 nodes, so space is O(n) in the worst case.

sections.cap: The queue is the key insight. If a problem asks for level-by-level processing on a tree, reach for a queue and the size-snapshot trick.

question: What is the difference between a binary tree and a heap?
title: Binary Tree vs Heap Java | Fresher Interview
direct_answer: A **heap** is a complete binary tree with the heap property: in a **min-heap**, every parent is smaller than its children (root = minimum). In a **max-heap**, every parent is larger (root = maximum). Java's `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap by default.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know heap structure and when to use PriorityQueue in Java
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing a BST with a heap — BST gives global sorted order; heap only guarantees parent-child relationship
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that heaps are stored in arrays (not explicit nodes) and that PriorityQueue is the go-to for top-k problems

sections.title: Heap = Complete Binary Tree + Heap Property
sections.content: A **binary tree** has no ordering constraint between siblings. A **BST** has left < root < right (global order). A **heap** has only a **parent-child order constraint**: min-heap: parent ≤ children; max-heap: parent ≥ children. Heaps are **complete binary trees** — filled level by level — which allows efficient array representation: left child at `2i+1`, right child at `2i+2`, parent at `(i-1)/2`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Min-heap: root = minimum, parent ≤ children
- Max-heap: root = maximum, parent ≥ children
- Heap operations: insert O(log n), extract-min/max O(log n), peek O(1)
- Stored in arrays — no explicit node objects
- Java PriorityQueue: min-heap by default
- Max-heap in Java: new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder())
- Use case: top-k elements, Dijkstra's shortest path, heap sort

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A heap is a special complete binary tree with a parent-child ordering constraint. In a min-heap the parent is always smaller than or equal to its children, so the root is always the minimum element. The key difference from a BST is that a heap only guarantees the parent-child relationship, not a global sorted order between siblings. In Java, PriorityQueue implements a min-heap and gives O(log n) insert and remove, and O(1) peek. I'd use it for top-k problems — like finding the k largest elements — or whenever I need efficient access to the minimum.

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app solving common interview DSA problems
sections.hook: Heaps and BSTs both involve ordered binary trees — but they guarantee very different things, and mixing them up is a red flag for interviewers.

beats.text: A plain binary tree has no ordering rule at all. A BST adds a global ordering rule: every node in the left subtree is smaller than the root, and every node in the right subtree is larger. A heap adds a completely different rule: only the parent-child relationship is ordered.
In a min-heap the root is always the minimum element and you can access it in O(1). Insert and extract-min both run in O(log n) because they re-heapify by swapping along a single path.

gotcha: heaps don't give you sorted order between siblings. You can't do an inorder traversal of a heap and get sorted output — that's a BST property. Heaps are optimized for one thing: fast access to the min or max.
In Java, PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default. For a max-heap pass Collections.reverseOrder() to the constructor. Use it for top-k problems, scheduling by priority, or Dijkstra's algorithm.

sections.cap: Choose a BST when you need sorted traversal or range queries. Choose a heap when you just need the min or max quickly.
